title: Funding for Talent: How to Use and Stack Programs to Grow Your Team
description: Funder and employer perspectives on talent programmes and combining eligible funding. Moderator: Elise Parsons.

summary.overview: Talent funding can help a small company hire a student, launch a research project or train an existing team—but the challenge is finding a programme that fits the actual work and applying early enough to use it. At techNL Summit, representatives of Mitacs, ICTC and the Government of Newfoundland and Labrador joined Copsys Technologies CEO Mike Maguire to discuss employer supports from both the funding and applicant sides. The strongest advice was to start with a hiring or innovation challenge rather than a subsidy, speak with programme advisers before preparing a finished application and plan months ahead. Panellists also described ways different programmes might support successive stages of a placement, subject to each funder’s rules and limits on total support.

keyTakeaways.heading: Define the work before choosing a funding programme
keyTakeaways.explanation: The panel distinguished research collaborations, digital-technology placements, summer jobs and workforce training. Eligibility depends on what a hire will actually do, which organization is hiring and the timing of the project. Programme representatives urged employers to discuss those facts with an adviser rather than selecting a fund simply because its name sounds relevant.

keyTakeaways.heading: Plan ahead and ask for help early
keyTakeaways.explanation: Copsys Technologies described the value of thinking about staffing needs several months in advance. Funders warned about applications submitted at the last minute, incomplete project scopes and changes that require applicants to start over. Advisers can help identify a suitable route before a proposal is fully polished.

keyTakeaways.heading: Combining supports is possible, but not automatic
keyTakeaways.explanation: Panellists discussed stacking or sequencing compatible programmes, including a research internship followed by another type of placement support. They cautioned that funders have different restrictions and that combined subsidies cannot simply exceed the eligible cost. Employers should confirm the terms with all organizations involved.

detailedSummary.heading: A toolkit rather than a single subsidy
paragraphs: The speakers represented different parts of the talent-development system. Mitacs described paid placements linking post-secondary talent with organizations working on research and innovation challenges, including its Accelerate and Business Strategy Internship programmes. ICTC discussed digital talent supports, while provincial officials outlined employment and skills-development assistance for employers and workers.

The panel repeatedly returned to the difference between a research project, a digital or back-office role, a summer placement and training for an existing employee. Those needs may point to different programmes, even when the employer is the same startup. The practical first step is to describe the work, the skill gap, the candidate and the desired outcome.

detailedSummary.heading: What the employer side looks like
paragraphs: Mike Maguire of Copsys Technologies spoke about using placements and hiring supports while building a technology company that operates across physical engineering systems and digital tools. For a small team, temporary placements offer a way to develop capability while learning how a prospective employee works within the business.

He also stressed the importance of looking ahead. When founders and early employees wear several hats, it is easy to focus only on immediate hiring needs. But funding applications, placements and eventual permanent hires are more useful when linked to a staffing plan for the next several months or year.

detailedSummary.heading: Stacking versus sequencing support
paragraphs: One question addressed whether companies can combine programmes. The response was cautiously positive: some funders allow compatible support from other sources, but each has restrictions. Speakers emphasized that the purpose is not to subsidize more than the actual eligible costs, and employers must verify whether combinations are permitted before assuming a placement is covered.

The panel offered the example of a Mitacs-supported project that might be followed by an ICTC-supported phase as a student continues working with the employer. That is a possible sequence, not a blanket rule or automatic approval. It illustrates why the timing, purpose and funding source of each stage matter.

detailedSummary.heading: Applications are a planning exercise
paragraphs: Funding representatives advised employers not to wait for a deadline—or until a chosen student needs to start—to ask questions. Project scope, academic or workplace supervision, programme review periods and available funding can all affect whether an application succeeds. A Mitacs placement, for example, involves both a company and an academic supervisor, so that support should be considered while defining the project.

The group also emphasized contacting local offices and industry advisers directly. The transcript mentioned that some programme information can be researched using AI tools, but participants were clear that speaking to the people administering the support is still valuable when interpreting eligibility and constraints.

detailedSummary.heading: Questions from startups, students and existing employers
paragraphs: Audience questions surfaced issues that do not disappear when a funding programme exists. One early-stage founder asked what support was realistic for a business without an established track record. The discussion acknowledged that some programmes have fewer such barriers than others, while upfront cash requirements and differences between programme and work-term durations can still create difficulties.

Speakers encouraged students and graduates to document their skills and projects, learn which supports employers might be able to use and bring that information into networking conversations. For employers focused on retention rather than new hiring, the panel pointed toward training partnerships and employee-development initiatives. These were pathways to investigate, not confirmed eligibility decisions for any particular attendee.

highlightedInsight.heading: Funding reduces risk only when it fits a real plan
highlightedInsight.explanation: The common thread was that a subsidy works best as one component of a hiring or innovation strategy. A well-defined task, appropriate mentoring and a realistic timeline matter alongside the amount a programme might contribute.

practicalApplications: Employer action: Write a one-page description of the work to be done, expected skills, supervision, candidate type and intended start date before approaching a programme adviser.
Employer action: Ask each potential funder explicitly whether other public or private support may be combined and how the eligible-cost ceiling is calculated.

Student action: If approaching a prospective employer, identify potentially relevant placement programmes but verify current eligibility, timing and available funding with the programme provider first.
notableIdeas: Mitacs highlighted research and business-innovation placements; ICTC and provincial officials discussed complementary talent and skills supports.
Participants emphasized that mentorship and adequate supervision are part of a successful placement, not optional details.
No subsidy amount, application window or programme eligibility mentioned in the recording should be treated as a current universal rule without checking the administering organization.
